lastRun.regime: Acute Hormuz supply shock: active mining and missile incidents, a US blockade, and a steep Brent backwardation, with the event study's escalation-fade rule as the only tested edge.
lastRun.summary: Hormuz tanker traffic is effectively halted and Brent is at $98.32 with M1-M12 backwardation of $17.73, so much of the disruption is already priced in. The desk is taking one small paper short in Brent on the escalation-fade rule, the only one that held out of sample, but that result is not statistically significant (9/14, p=0.21). The live AIS zero counts and the PortWatch data (last date 2026-06-09) are stale or inconsistent with the headlines, so neither is used.

ideas.label: Brent crude (ICE, front month)
ideas.thesis: Escalation premium in Brent has historically faded over about 20 trading days, and the steep backwardation already prices heavy near-term disruption. A short with a 28-day horizon targets that fade, with the stop placed beyond the 2.7% daily noise over the window.
evidence: Live prices: Brent 98.32, M1-M12 spread 17.73 (desk futures curve)
Event study escalation 20d median for BRENT -3.79%, up 3/11
Walk-forward BRENT 20d rule: hits 9/14, avg net +1.32, buy-and-hold net -2.63, p=0.212 (not significant)
Reuters via gCaptain 2026-11-06: tanker rates soaring, freight and discount dynamics tied to the Iran conflict
Headlines: Iran says Hormuz stays closed until US accepts 7 conditions (official position); Qatari plan could reopen the strait (unverified mediation proposal)
Headlines: Trump confirms new US strikes near Hormuz (White House statement, relayed)
ideas.invalidation: A close above about 108 (roughly +10% from 98.32) on confirmed strikes on Gulf export infrastructure or a further Hormuz escalation, or a sustained rise in the M1-M2 spread that signals the physical squeeze is intensifying rather than fading.

ai.reading: The state-strike escalation history favours a 20-day fade, but the walk-forward result is not significant and the current event is an ongoing closure rather than a one-off spike, so I size it small and treat the probability as only modestly above a coin flip.

backtest.method: Same prompt, schema, maths and risk checks as the live desk. Point-in-time inputs only. Entry at the first daily close after the news; stops/targets checked on daily closes; round-trip costs charged. Book P&L = R x risk% of book.
backtest.caveat: The model may already know how these events played out from its training data, which would flatter these results. Treat this as a test of the machinery and of calibration; the live paper record is the only truly unseen test.
